messages.author: f9c6a2087c744460
messages.subject: Question about the weights option
parts:
Hi,

So I'm thinking to build a model with simulated data, and I was wondering could I use weights. Essentially, I'm simulate case control data where the cases are rare. Lets say I might have 2000 controls for each case. I could simulate 2000 controls with essentially the same variables, but I was wondering could I simulate 1 control and weight it x2000 relative to the 1 case - hopefully this would be faster when I have 1000 cases and 2 million controls for example. Anyhow, I was looking at the documentation and found the following dire warnings about weights:

Fixed (optional) weights parameters of the likelihood, so the log-likelihood[i] is changed into weights[i]*log-likelihood[i]. Default value is rep(1, n.data). Due to the danger of mis-interpreting the results (see below), this option is DISABLED by default. You can enable this option for the rest of your R session, doing inla.setOption(enable.inla.argument.weights=TRUE). WARNING: The normalizing constant for the likelihood is NOT recomputed, so ALL marginals (and the marginal likelihood) must be interpreted with great care. Possibly, you may want to set the prior for the hyperparameters to "uniform" and the integration strategy to "eb" to mimic a maximum-likelihood approach.

Weighting the likelihood sounds like what I want to do, but I'm not sure what "interpreted with great care" implies ? My best guess is this is due to the normalising constant not being recomputed so therefore model parameters are off ? What is the advantage of setting uniform priors and the "eb" integrations strategy ?

I hope this question makes sense - apologies if not I'm still thinking this through

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Question about the weights option
parts:
Hi,

2000 simulated data points is _not_ equivalent to 1 data point with
weight 2000, since you'd be leaving out all the random variability
between the samples and amplifying the one single data point. Yes, it
would be faster, but I'd expect the results to be very very wrong.
Otherwise we'd be doing this all the time; why use a large data set if
you could simply take a single data point and repeat it with no ill
effect? Consider a sample x_1,...,x_n ~ N(mu, sigma^2). How would you
estimate the variance sigma^2 if you only used x_1, with likelihood
weighted by a factor n? It would be equivalent to just repeating x_1 n
times, which would give empirical variance exactly equal to zero.
Clearly not right.

The uniform+eb comment is there due to the most common use case of
"weights" is to mimic a certain frequentistic method, and that makes
it close to that.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Question about the weights option
parts:
Hi Finn,

Yes good point, but perhaps I didn't' explain very well.

I'm working with a BYM2 model with about 2200 cases from a population of 4million over 23 years. Until now I've been working with obersved counts pre totalled per area with expected counts based on census data per polygon. But I was wondering if I could work with individual data by simulating controls based on the census counts per area. But if I simulate all of them and wanted to do space time analysis says thats 92million simulated controls which seem a tad excessive. So then I thought I could simulate a represented sample. so for example if there were 40,000 females aged 40-45yr nationally, I was thinking to simulate 4000 of them in a spatial pattern representative of my census counts per polygon. But then it occurred to me that my denominator would be wrong - hence I was thinking about weights. But you raise good point. While the 40,000 would have the same variables for gender and age, I hadn't thought that their spatial variables differ. (although I could calculate a more complex weight including the national population of 40-45yr females and the per polygon population of 40-45yr females).

Anyway, thanks for your answer!

On Mon, 2019-01-14 at 14:00 -0800, jpkrooney wrote:

> Weighting the likelihood sounds like what I want to do, but I'm not
> sure what "interpreted with great care" implies ? My best guess is
> this is due to the normalising constant not being recomputed so
> therefore model parameters are off ? What is the advantage of setting
> uniform priors and the "eb" integrations strategy ?

Just to add some more to this than Finn has already done.
The 'weighting' of the likelihood is a very special option, and
not ment to be used unless you *know* that this is what you want.
Otherwise, this is very likely not what you want. This is the motivation
for this option to be 'enabled' by the user before use.


--
